newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMAN RATES SEEN STEADY AS MARCH M3 GROWTH SLOWS.
newsitem.headline: GERMAN RATES SEEN STEADY AS MARCH M3 GROWTH SLOWS.

text.p: German M3 money supply growth, one of the Bundesbank's main indicators, slowed in March but remained above target, reinforcing analysts' predictions of unchanged interest rates for the rest of 1997.

Data released on Tuesday showed a steep rise in bank lending to the public sector of 14.1 billion marks ($8.3 billion). But analysts expect government borrowing to slow in the coming months as Bonn tries to trim its budget deficit to qualify for Europe's planned monetary union.
The Bundesbank said M3 expanded at an annualised, seasonally-adjusted rate of 8.3 percent in March compared with growth of 9.1 percent in February.

The March rate matched analysts' forecasts. It had little impact on the German bond market which weakened in sympathy with French bonds due to expectations that France will announce an early general election on Monday evening.

Growth in the stock of money, regarded as a forward indicator of inflationary trends, remained above the Bundesbank's target range of 3.5 to 6.5 percent in March. But economists expect it to keep decelerating in the coming months.

That slowdown, together with tame inflation data and an economic recovery which still seems fragile, should preclude any rise in German interest rates from their current historic lows for the time being, economists say.
The central bank's main money market rate, or repo, has been fixed at three percent since August.
At the same time economists regard a decline in Bundesbank interest rates as unlikely given that the German recovery is slowly gathering steam.
A rate cut could also encourage the mark to continue falling against the dollar, a drop which the Bundesbank only last week reiterated had gone far enough.
"I doubt that the economic environment will require a change in interest rates much before the end of the year," said Uwe Angenendt, an economist at BHF-Bank in Frankfurt.
"But I wouldn't rule out an interest rate rise at the end of the year or in early 1998."

While March money supply growth was fuelled by public borrowing and by a decline in fresh investment in bonds, the expansion was reined in by slower bank lending to the private sector, the Bundesbank said.
Germany also saw a net outflow of money as foreign investors sold mark-denominated securities, helping to curtail growth in the amount of money circulating in the economy.

The Bundesbank said investment in bonds fell sharply to 7.6 billion marks in March from 17.0 billion in February. Investment in bonds, known as money capital formation, dampens money supply growth because it involves the withdrawal of funds from M3.
That drop, the Bundesbank said, was caused by a rise in bond yields during March which had unsettled investors.
But economists expect money capital formation to rise in the coming months as the bond market becomes less volatile and yields stabilise at higher levels.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year German New Year government bond, or Bund, rose to 5.85 percent by 1130 GMT from Friday's closing rate of 5.83 percent.
Yields are expected to climb beyond six percent by the end of the year as German economic growth picks up and amid expectations of higher U.S. interest rates.
The Bundesbank's M3 money supply aggregate comprises cash in circulation, sight deposits, time deposits and short-term savings deposits.
Separately, the Statistics Office reported that pan-German producer prices were unchanged in March month-on-month and rose 0.7 percent year-on-year. The figures were slightly weaker than expected.
